noun: A word for a thing, a person or a place: house, man, city. In Dutch: huis, man, stad.
article: The small word before a noun. English: the, a. Dutch: de, het, een.
adjective: A word that describes a noun: big, small, beautiful. In Dutch: groot, klein, mooi.
infinitive: The full, basic form of a verb, as you find it in the dictionary: werken (to work), gaan (to go).
stem: The short base form of a Dutch verb. Take the infinitive and remove -en: werken becomes werk.
conjugate: To change a verb so it fits the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. The conjugated verb is the changed form.
participle: The verb form you use after hebben or zijn: gewerkt, gegaan. Like English 'worked' in 'I have worked'.
modal: A helper verb: kunnen (can), moeten (must), mogen (may), willen (want), zullen (will). It always works together with a second verb.
particle: The small first part of a separable verb: the op in opstaan, the mee in meenemen.
prefix: A fixed first part of a word, like be- in betalen. It cannot stand alone.
vowel: One of the letters a, e, i, o, u, or a pair like aa, oo, ui. Long vowel: aa in maan. Short vowel: a in man.
consonant: Every letter that is not a vowel: b, k, s, t, and so on.
stress: The part of a word you say with the most force. In OPstaan the stress is on op. Unstressed means: said without force.
diminutive: The 'small form' of a noun, made with -je: huis becomes huisje (little house).
pronoun: A small word used in place of a name or noun: ik (I), jij (you), hij (he).
subject: The person or thing that does the action: IK werk (I work).
object: The person or thing that receives the action: Ik zie JOU (I see YOU).
possessive: A word that says whose something is: mijn (my), jouw (your), ons (our).
preposition: A small word for place or time: in, op, aan, om, bij.
relative-clause: Extra information about a noun, inside the sentence: the man WHO LIVES THERE. In Dutch: de man DIE DAAR WOONT.
main-clause: A part of a sentence that can stand alone as a full sentence: Ik blijf thuis (I stay home).
subordinate-clause: A part of a sentence that cannot stand alone. It starts with a word like omdat: ...omdat ik ziek ben (...because I am sick).
clause: A part of a sentence with its own verb.
inversion: The subject and the verb change places: ik ga becomes ga ik.
definite: One specific, known thing: de auto (that exact car). The opposite of indefinite.
indefinite: Not one specific thing: een auto (a car, any car). The opposite of definite.
negate: To make a sentence say 'not': Ik werk (I work) becomes Ik werk niet (I do NOT work).
comparative: The 'more' form of an adjective: groter (bigger), mooier (more beautiful).
superlative: The 'most' form of an adjective: grootst (biggest), mooist (most beautiful).
passive: A sentence where the subject does not do the action but receives it: Het huis wordt gebouwd (the house is being built).
weak-verb: A verb with a regular past form: werken, werkte, gewerkt.
strong-verb: A verb that changes its vowel in the past: drinken, dronk, gedronken. You must learn these one by one.
phrasal-verb: An English verb made of two words, like 'pick up' or 'get up'.
separable-verb: A Dutch verb that can break in two parts: opstaan becomes ik sta op. See the Separable Verbs topic.
irregular: Does not follow the normal rule. You must learn it by heart.
gender: The group of a noun. Every Dutch noun is a de-word or a het-word.
